TUOL SLENG, Cambodia (CNN)  -- The trial of a former prison chief with the Khmer Rouge movement resumed inside a packed Cambodian courtroom Monday, with prosecutors painting a grim picture of inmates who were electrocuted, whipped and beaten to death. Duch ran a prison where people were tortured and killed under the Khmer Rouge. Kaing Guek Eav, a former math teacher and a born-again Christian, displayed no emotion as the U.N.-backed tribunal accused him not just of overseeing the torture and killing of more than 15,000 men, women and children three decades ago -- but of actively taking part in some of them. The trial of the 66-year-old man, better known as Duch, resumed Monday just outside the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh. Spectators, many of them survivors of the abuse, watched the proceedings from an auditorium separated from the courtroom by a large glass window. The proceedings began with Duch offering a basic introduction of himself. Court officials then read out the findings of their lengthy investigation. Prosecutors contend Duch ran S-21, a prison that had been converted from a school. Here, men, women and children were shackled to iron beds and tortured -- before they were beaten to death, prosecutors said. Many of the victims were military officials or Communist Party members targeted for not going along with the philosophy of the ultra-Maoist Khmer Rouge movement, prosecutors said. Duch faces charges that include crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture and murder. He has admitted his role in the Khmer Rouge's genocidal reign.  Watch why his trial is significant » . The movement swept to power in 1975. Three years, eight months and 20 days later, at least 1.7 million people -- nearly one-quarter of Cambodia's population -- were dead from execution, disease, starvation and overwork, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. The non-profit organization has been at the forefront of recording the atrocities committed during the Khmer Rouge regime. S-21 was one of 189 similar institutions across Cambodia. Duch is the first former Khmer Rouge leader to stand trial. The tribunal, which is made up of Cambodian and international judges, does not have the power to impose the death penalty. If convicted, Duch faces from five years to life in prison. The trial is expected to last three or four months. "Probably the most important thing about this court is: even after 35 years, you are still not going to get away with it. That is the message," said Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit. Even though Duch was not a senior leader with the movement, many Cambodians were relieved that one of the regime's former leaders was facing justice, said Youk Chhang, head of the Documentation Center of Cambodia. "I think there is a feeling of, well you know, finally -- now it's finally happening after all these years of waiting -- hearing, fighting, negotiating," he told CNN last month. "People have that kind of sense of relief that it's now moving. When I ask people around the center today, people say, 'Oh, it's about time.'" Four of the regime's former leaders, also accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, await trial before the tribunal. The regime's leader, Pol Pot, died in 1998. "It all seems so fresh," said Norng Champhal, who was a starving little boy when Vietnamese forces invaded the prison. He was separated from his mother after a night in the prison and never saw her again. "It's hard to control my feelings when I see this," he said, as he watched footage of the prison taken 30 years ago. "I wonder whether my parents were tortured like these people," he said. CNN's Dan Rivers contributed to this report.

**Trial Resumes for Former Khmer Rouge Prison Chief Duch**

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — The trial of Kaing Guek Eav, better known as Duch, the former chief of the Khmer Rouge’s notorious S-21 prison, resumed before Cambodia’s U.N.-backed war crimes tribunal, bringing renewed attention to one of the darkest chapters in the country’s history.

Duch, who ran the Tuol Sleng prison in Phnom Penh during the Khmer Rouge regime, is charged with crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture and murder. Prosecutors say he oversaw a system in which more than 12,000 men, women and children were imprisoned, tortured and sent to their deaths between 1975 and 1979.

Only a handful of prisoners are believed to have survived S-21.

The proceedings are being heard by the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, a hybrid tribunal established by Cambodia and the United Nations to try senior leaders and those most responsible for atrocities committed under the Khmer Rouge.

Tribunal officials said the resumption of the case marks a significant moment for survivors and families of victims who have waited decades for accountability.

“This trial is an important step in the search for justice for the Cambodian people,” a tribunal official said. “It is also part of the historical record of what happened under Democratic Kampuchea.”

Duch, a former mathematics teacher, has admitted his role at S-21 but has argued that he was acting under orders from senior Khmer Rouge leaders. During earlier hearings, he expressed remorse for his actions, telling the court he accepted responsibility for crimes committed at the prison.

Survivors, however, say apologies cannot erase the suffering endured inside Tuol Sleng, where prisoners were photographed, interrogated and forced to confess to crimes before being executed.

“For many of us, this is not only about punishment,” said one survivor who attended the hearing. “It is about the truth being spoken in court, so the next generation will know what happened.”

The Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, seized power in 1975 and attempted to create an agrarian communist utopia. Cities were emptied, money was abolished, schools and religious institutions were shut down, and millions were forced into labor camps. An estimated 1.7 million people died from execution, starvation, disease and overwork before the regime was overthrown in 1979.

Tuol Sleng, now a genocide museum, remains one of the most powerful symbols of the regime’s brutality. Former classrooms were converted into cells and interrogation rooms, and thousands of prisoner photographs line the walls.

Human rights advocates say Duch’s trial is significant because it is the first major case involving a senior Khmer Rouge figure to move forward after years of delays, political disputes and legal challenges.

“The Cambodian people have waited a very long time to see those responsible brought before a court,” one human rights observer said. “Even if justice comes late, it still matters.”

Prosecutors are expected to continue presenting evidence about Duch’s command role at S-21, including prison records, witness testimony and documents recovered after the fall of the Khmer Rouge.

Defense lawyers are expected to argue that Duch was not among the regime’s top decision-makers and that he feared for his own life if he disobeyed orders.

For families of the dead, the trial is a rare opportunity to confront the machinery of a regime that devastated Cambodia and left scars that remain visible across the country.

As the hearing resumed, Buddhist monks, survivors and relatives of victims gathered outside the tribunal, some holding photographs of loved ones lost more than three decades ago.

“We cannot bring them back,” a relative of an S-21 victim said. “But we can ask the court to remember them, and to judge the man who helped take them away.”

**TUOL SLENG, Cambodia —** In the silent classrooms of the former S-21 prison, where rusting bedframes, iron shackles and black-and-white photographs still testify to one of the darkest chapters of the 20th century, Cambodia is confronting a long-delayed reckoning.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary alias **Duch**, is on trial before a United Nations-backed tribunal for his role as commandant of **Security Prison 21**, the Khmer Rouge torture and execution center now preserved as the **Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum** in Phnom Penh.

The proceedings mark the first major trial of a senior Khmer Rouge figure before the **Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia**, a hybrid Cambodian-international court created to prosecute those most responsible for atrocities committed during the regime’s rule from 1975 to 1979.

Duch, a former mathematics teacher turned prison chief, is accused of overseeing a system in which detainees were interrogated, tortured, forced to confess to imagined crimes, and then sent for execution. Prosecutors say more than **12,000 men, women and children** passed through S-21. Only a small number survived.

At Tuol Sleng, the evidence is almost unbearably visible. The compound, once a high school, was transformed by the Khmer Rouge into a secret prison. Classrooms became cells and torture chambers. Prisoners were photographed upon arrival, catalogued, interrogated and, in most cases, killed. Many were taken to the nearby **Choeung Ek killing fields**, where mass graves later revealed the scale of the slaughter.

Duch has admitted responsibility for many of the crimes committed at S-21, a rare acknowledgment among former Khmer Rouge officials. In court, he has expressed remorse and asked forgiveness from victims’ families, while also arguing that he acted under orders and feared for his own life if he disobeyed.

Prosecutors, however, say Duch was not merely a subordinate but a willing and efficient administrator of terror. They allege he refined interrogation procedures, maintained meticulous records, and reported directly to senior Khmer Rouge leaders.

The trial has drawn survivors, monks, students, journalists and relatives of victims to the court and to Tuol Sleng itself. For many Cambodians, the proceedings are not only about one man’s guilt, but about whether justice can still be achieved decades after the fall of the Khmer Rouge.

Between 1975 and 1979, the Khmer Rouge, led by **Pol Pot**, sought to create an agrarian communist society by emptying cities, abolishing money and religion, and forcing millions into rural labor camps. An estimated **1.7 million people** died from execution, starvation, disease and overwork.

For years after the regime’s collapse, many of its senior leaders lived freely or remained politically protected. The U.N.-backed tribunal was established after lengthy negotiations between Cambodia and the international community, but it has faced criticism over delays, cost, political interference and the advanced age of the defendants.

Still, for survivors of S-21, Duch’s trial carries profound symbolic weight. It is the first time the machinery of the Khmer Rouge security system has been examined in a court of law with extensive documentation, witness testimony and participation from civil parties.

Inside Tuol Sleng, visitors move quietly past walls covered with portraits of prisoners — young men, elderly women, children, cadres accused of betrayal, entire families swallowed by the paranoia of the regime. Their images form one of the most extensive archives of state terror ever preserved.

The tribunal’s judgment in Duch’s case is expected to set an important precedent for later proceedings against other surviving Khmer Rouge leaders. But here, amid the barred windows and faded floors of S-21, the legal questions are inseparable from memory.

For Cambodia, Duch’s trial is a confrontation with a place where bureaucracy and brutality became one — and where, decades later, the demand for justice still echoes through the empty rooms.

The Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, sought to create an agrarian communist society, emptying cities, abolishing money and religion, and forcing millions into labor camps.

An estimated 1.7 million Cambodians died from execution, starvation, disease and overwork before the regime was toppled in 1979.

For many Cambodians, Duch’s trial represents more than a legal reckoning. It is the first major test of the long-delayed tribunal and a symbolic moment for survivors who have waited decades for accountability. The proceedings also mark one of the few times that a figure directly connected to the Khmer Rouge security apparatus has been compelled to answer publicly for the crimes committed in its name.

**First Khmer Rouge Leader Stands Trial Over Tuol Sleng Atrocities**

*Phnom Penh, Cambodia* — The first Khmer Rouge figure to face trial before a United Nations-backed tribunal has been accused of overseeing one of the regime’s most notorious killing machines: the Tuol Sleng prison, where thousands of men, women and children were tortured before being sent to their deaths.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary alias **Duch**, appeared before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, the hybrid tribunal established to prosecute senior Khmer Rouge leaders and those most responsible for crimes committed during the regime’s 1975-1979 rule.

Duch, a former mathematics teacher turned prison chief, ran **Security Prison 21**, commonly known as **S-21** or Tuol Sleng, in Phnom Penh. The former high school was converted by the Khmer Rouge into a secret detention and interrogation center where suspected enemies of the revolution were photographed, shackled, tortured and forced to sign confessions before being executed.

Prosecutors allege that Duch played a central role in the prison’s operation, overseeing a system of interrogation, forced confessions and executions. They say he supervised staff, approved torture methods, maintained detailed records and ensured that prisoners were sent to the nearby **Choeung Ek killing fields**, where most were killed and buried in mass graves.

An estimated **12,000 to 14,000 people** passed through Tuol Sleng. Only a small number are known to have survived.

Duch faces charges including **crimes against humanity**, **war crimes**, torture and murder. Prosecutors argue that Tuol Sleng was not a rogue facility but a key institution in the Khmer Rouge security apparatus, designed to identify and eliminate perceived traitors within the party, the military, government ministries and the wider population.

“This was a place where people entered and almost never came out alive,” prosecutors told the court, describing Duch as a disciplined and efficient administrator who “knew exactly what was happening” inside the prison. They said the accused was not merely following orders, but actively managed the machinery of terror.

Duch has admitted that he ran Tuol Sleng and has expressed remorse, but his defense has argued that he acted under orders from senior Khmer Rouge leaders and feared he would be killed if he disobeyed. His lawyers have sought to portray him as a subordinate within a brutal chain of command, rather than one of the architects of the regime’s crimes.

For survivors, the trial marks a long-awaited moment of reckoning.

**Chum Mey**, one of the few people to survive S-21, said the proceedings were an opportunity to confront the man responsible for his suffering and the deaths of so many others. Chum Mey survived because he was useful to prison staff as a mechanic. He has described being tortured and hearing the screams of other prisoners during interrogations.

Another survivor, **Bou Meng**, who was kept alive because he could paint portraits of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, has said he wants the court to establish the truth for victims and their families. Like other survivors, he has attended hearings not only to seek justice, but to bear witness to what happened inside Tuol Sleng.

Outside the courtroom, civil parties and relatives of victims said the trial could never fully compensate for the loss of entire families, but they hoped it would provide an official record of the crimes and help younger Cambodians understand the scale of the Khmer Rouge’s brutality.

The Khmer Rouge ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979, during which an estimated **1.7 million people** died from execution, starvation, disease and forced labor. The regime emptied cities, abolished money and private property, and attempted to create an agrarian communist utopia through violence and mass coercion.

Tuol Sleng became one of the most chilling symbols of that era. Prisoners included former Khmer Rouge cadres accused of betrayal, intellectuals, workers, diplomats, soldiers, foreigners and even children. The prison’s surviving records — including photographs, confessions and execution lists — have become crucial evidence for investigators.

Prosecutors say those records show Duch’s direct involvement in the fate of detainees. Many confessions were annotated, and prison documents detailed the movement of prisoners from interrogation rooms to execution sites. The prosecution argues that Duch’s command was methodical and that his role was indispensable to the prison’s function.

The trial is being closely watched in Cambodia and abroad as the tribunal’s first major test. For years, many victims feared that senior Khmer Rouge figures would die before facing justice. Pol Pot died in 1998 without being tried. Other top leaders lived freely for years after the movement collapsed.

Duch’s trial is expected to set the tone for future cases against more senior surviving Khmer Rouge leaders. But for many Cambodians, the case is deeply personal: it is the first time a key figure from the regime has been required to answer publicly for the horrors that unfolded in one of its most infamous prisons.

As testimony continues, survivors say they want more than punishment. They want acknowledgment.

“We want the truth,” one civil party said outside the court. “We want the world to know what happened at Tuol Sleng, and we want the victims to be remembered.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a breaking-news-style CNN report on the trial of former Khmer Rouge prison chief Kaing Guek Eav, including background on Pol Pot’s regime, the tribunal, possible sentencing, and eyewitness survivor comments.
counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS-STYLE REPORT**

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia —** The former chief of the Khmer Rouge’s most notorious prison is on trial in Cambodia, facing charges linked to the torture and deaths of thousands during one of the 20th century’s darkest chapters.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary alias **Duch**, headed the secret prison known as **S-21**, or **Tuol Sleng**, in Phnom Penh. Prosecutors say more than **12,000 men, women and children** were imprisoned there under the Khmer Rouge regime, tortured into giving confessions, and then executed at nearby killing fields. Only a handful are known to have survived.

Duch is being tried before the **Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia**, a United Nations-backed tribunal created to prosecute senior Khmer Rouge leaders and those most responsible for atrocities committed between **1975 and 1979**.

### Background: Pol Pot’s Regime

The Khmer Rouge, led by **Pol Pot**, seized power in Cambodia in April 1975 and renamed the country **Democratic Kampuchea**. The regime attempted to create an agrarian communist utopia by emptying cities, abolishing money and private property, forcing people into rural labor camps, and targeting intellectuals, professionals, religious minorities and perceived enemies.

An estimated **1.7 million people** died from execution, starvation, disease and forced labor before Vietnamese forces toppled the regime in January 1979.

Tuol Sleng became a central part of the Khmer Rouge’s machinery of terror. Prisoners were photographed, interrogated and tortured. Many were accused of being spies for foreign powers. After forced confessions, they were often taken to **Choeung Ek**, now known as one of Cambodia’s “killing fields,” where they were executed.

### The Trial

Duch has admitted that he ran S-21, but the central legal questions include the extent of his responsibility, whether he acted under orders, and what punishment he should face.

He is charged with crimes including **crimes against humanity**, **war crimes**, torture and murder. Prosecutors argue that Duch was not merely a functionary, but an active and meticulous administrator of mass killing.

Duch has expressed remorse in court, asking victims’ families for forgiveness. But many survivors and relatives say apology is not enough.

### Possible Sentencing

If convicted, Duch could face a lengthy prison sentence, potentially **life imprisonment**, depending on the tribunal’s findings. At the time of the trial, the court is also weighing time he has already spent in detention.

The case is widely seen as a test of whether Cambodia’s long-delayed tribunal can deliver justice more than three decades after the fall of the Khmer Rouge.

### Survivor Reactions

Survivors of S-21 have attended the proceedings, some confronting Duch in court.

**Chum Mey**, one of the few known survivors of Tuol Sleng, has said he still carries the trauma of what happened there and wants the court to recognize the suffering of victims. He survived because he had mechanical skills useful to the prison staff.

Another survivor, **Bou Meng**, whose wife was killed after they were imprisoned, has also demanded accountability, saying the trial is important not only for survivors but for younger Cambodians who need to understand what happened.

For many Cambodians, the trial is both a legal reckoning and a national moment of remembrance.

### A Nation Still Living With the Past

The tribunal has faced criticism over delays, cost, and the limited number of defendants brought to justice. Many former Khmer Rouge members lived freely for years after the regime collapsed, and Pol Pot himself died in 1998 without ever facing trial.

Still, Duch’s case marks the first major prosecution of a Khmer Rouge figure before an internationalized court.

For survivors and families of the dead, the proceedings offer a rare public accounting of a system that turned schools into prisons, neighbors into informants, and Cambodia into a country of mass graves.

**The verdict, when it comes, will not erase the suffering — but for many, it may finally put an official judgment on crimes Cambodia has lived with for more than a generation.**
